narrative:
The model predicted a 77.4% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is quite high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three pieces of information about your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest factor and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the second decile, noticeably lower than the average ranking of accepted students. Your first-year ranking was the third most important factor and similarly pulled the outcome toward failure; again you stood in the second decile while accepted students averaged around the sixth.

Your LSAT score worked in the opposite direction. At 43 it is higher than the average of 37 among accepted applicants, which gave a meaningful boost toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the two weaker academic rankings.

Gender, race, family income, undergraduate GPA, and planned full-time status played no meaningful role in the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and class standing in law school if you retake courses or enroll elsewhere. Raising your standing in the upper half of your class would likely change the prediction substantially. Consider reapplying once you have evidence of stronger performance.
